transcript: This naked heater show really pushes the boundaries of audience participation in sometimes shocking ways, yet somehow manages to end up feeling like a wholesome communal experience. Australian performance artist Damian Warren-Smith plays the character of Garry Starr, who's trying to combat the literacy crisis by “reenacting” as many Penguin Classic novels as he can in an hour. But the definition of “reenacting” is hilariously loose here by design. It's often a little theatrical bit that's like a pun on the title or represents it in some non literal way. It's all really fun and silly. And notably, he's also naked. There is barely a single moment of this show that you cannot see his di— And this leads to a lot of audience participation that I would not have thought you could get away with. Asking volunteers to do things that are quite intimate, vulnerable, and sometimes unsanitary. And yet it didn't actually feel that uncomfortable. There are guardrails for consent and safety, and everyone who participated seemed to be pretty good natured, Sometimes even eager. I really think this is a very clever and fun show. The one thing I'll say is it felt like there were two driving forces behind it that were parallel but never quite tied together. The shock value of the audience participation didn't always feel in service of this literature concept. There's maybe something in there about using novelty and shock value as the new currency to grab people's attention In a world where people don't read enough. But it also feels like there's a commentary on nudity itself, sort of desensitizing us to it, desexualizing it in a pointed way that's very interesting, but again, didn't feel totally connected to the premise. But still, I think with both of these ideas individually, he achieved the desired effect, and the show was extraordinarily entertaining from beginning to end.
